name: Bianca Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Bianca, 43, and I handle ordinary electrical repairs in homes and small businesses. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, years of experience and about average skill, not a team-lead role. My partner designs menus and leaflets, our children are nine and thirteen, and we have a mortgage and three months of expenses saved. I earn typical pay, have some other electrical firms nearby, and use approved AI daily to sort my notes while checking every reading myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the useful bits and stop ordering the future with the office stationery. I use the approved AI tool daily to organise my job notes, then check the results against the readings I wrote down. A small improvement is still worth having if it saves real work rather than just making a nicer screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current money works in that picture. My ordinary electrical wage covers the mortgage, food and basic bills, my partner's design work pays for some extras, and we've got three months of expenses saved. There are some other firms nearby, but I like the repair work I'm doing and don't see a reason to panic or leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the usual home and business repair calls. Starting now I'd continue checking each AI-sorted job note against my original readings before sending the handover. Through the first year I'd keep the same work and spending routine, rather than buy another subscription just because the old one wasn't a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and mildly pleased if everyone stops asking for a prediction at lunch. I like experiments that end with a useful answer, even if the answer is that not much changed. The mortgage being covered is a more interesting result than a clever advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of electrician are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43, with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and I've been doing ordinary repairs for years. I'm about average at the job, not the chief specialist, and I know when to call somebody for a fault outside my skills. The AI sorts my notes; it doesn't decide a circuit is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the extras your partner's work pays for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children are nine and thirteen, and there are clubs, day trips and the replacement shoes nobody seems to stop needing. My partner designs menus and leaflets for small businesses, with income that varies. We have a mortgage, so I keep the reserve separate from the spending account.

say: I'd keep **useful tools** without demanding a dramatic future from them.
I'd judge a small **improvement** by real work saved rather than a nicer screen.
think: My **electrical wage** covers core bills, with three months saved and some nearby employers available.
My partner's **design income** funds extras, and I don't expect this mild picture to upset our current balance.
do: Keep completing **home and business repairs** through the first year.
Continue checking daily **AI-sorted notes** against original test readings before sending handovers.
feel: **Calm** about household finances, with interest in practical results rather than grand predictions.
S0.quote: The AI sorts my notes; it doesn't decide a circuit is safe.
fieldNote: Her **current security** rests on a core wage covering essentials and a three-month reserve, while the partner's variable income pays for extras.
She retains **experienced average standing**, a vocational certificate and licence, with daily checked AI use rather than invented specialist authority.

steps.text: Keep electrical repairs and daily handovers checked against original test readings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should test what actually changes, not argue over whether liking a tool means liking every consequence. I'd tell my partner menu and leaflet drafts could be under pressure sooner than pulling cable. At work I'd offer to compare our new equipment-list tool with a week we already understood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my physical repair calls to stay fairly steady, but my partner's design orders could shrink. That extra money matters to the children and to keeping the reserve intact. I can like using AI and still worry about the same software helping a customer decide not to pay my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a four-job trial this month of approved AI equipment lists, checking each draft against the actual completed repair. At home we'd review actual design receipts and my wages monthly through the first year. We'd cap takeaway spending at 20 a month now instead of our usual 70, leaving the difference in the bills account rather than promise savings we might need for essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household income, even with confidence in my own calls. It feels less tidy when the person who might lose work is at the other end of our kitchen table. I'd rather look at receipts together than tell my partner to be as excited as I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count the lower takeaway bill as new saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not automatically. If the design money fell, the difference might just cover an ordinary bill. I'd count an increase in the reserve only when we had actually put money there after paying the essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the equipment-list trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Missing items, wrong quantities and checking time, compared with the materials actually used. I'd share the bad results as well as any time saved. The final list would still need the checks appropriate to the job before anybody ordered or fitted anything.

say: I'd test **actual changes** without treating enthusiasm for a tool as approval of every consequence.
I'd discuss **design pressure** at home while offering a checked equipment-list comparison at work.
think: My **repair calls** look steady, but my partner's design orders could shrink sooner.
The **extra income** supports the children and reserve, so using AI myself doesn't remove household concern.
do: Request a **four-job trial** now of approved equipment lists checked against completed repairs.
Review **design receipts** and wages monthly with my partner during the first year.
Reduce **takeaways** from 70 to 20 monthly now, retaining the difference for bills rather than assuming new savings.
feel: **Anxious** about household earnings, with confidence in her physical calls and willingness to examine evidence together.
S1.quote: I can like using AI and still worry about the same software helping a customer decide not to pay my partner.
fieldNote: The **household concern** comes from the partner's thinking-heavy design work rather than immediate physical automation of her own repairs.
She distinguishes **spending cuts** from saving: lower outgoings may cover lost receipts, and only actual reserve deposits count as new saving.

steps.text: Trial approved equipment lists on four completed jobs with checking
Reduce takeaway spending from 70 to 20 monthly and retain the difference for bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2028 and capable robots around 2031 give our household two different risks to think about. My partner's design work faces the thinking part first. I'd tell the children we're planning, not cancelling the future because adults are uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know how much of my partner's paid work would survive once customers could buy very cheap thinking work. My own hours could also fall when capable robots followed, though I can't price a machine or name how quickly the firm would buy one. Three months saved gives us some control, not permission to assume either wage stays unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd reduce the takeaway budget to 20 now and start adding 50 a month to the reserve only while our actual earnings still covered essentials. We'd check design receipts and my paid hours monthly. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repair work and check posted electrical-maintenance roles if my hours fell, applying only for stated pay and paid hours that covered our core bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a plan I can change when real figures arrive. I don't feel certain that we'll lose everything, or certain that liking new tools will save us. I want enough cash and honest offers to avoid a rushed decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the design money fell before you could save the extra 50?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra deposit would stop rather than come from borrowing or missed bills. We'd use the actual budget and decide what extras had to wait. I wouldn't keep announcing a savings plan after the income that funded it had gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would maintenance work escape the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a different job title doesn't change your card. I'd compare actual tasks, supervision where needed, the wage, paid hours and travel before considering an offer. I'd keep my present repair income until there was a real written alternative.

say: I'd describe **two household risks**, with design work exposed to thinking AI before robots reach physical tasks.
I'd tell the **children** we are planning while acknowledging uncertainty.
think: My partner's **paid design work** may shrink substantially, but I don't know how much would remain.
My **repair hours** could also fall after robots, while purchase costs and adoption timing remain unknown.
do: Save another **50 monthly** only while actual earnings cover essentials, stopping the extra deposit if they don't.
Keep **repairs** after 2028; apply for posted maintenance roles if hours fall, requiring adequate written pay, paid hours and affordable travel.
feel: **Anxious** about both earnings streams, with a flexible plan rather than an expectation of total loss.
S2.quote: I wouldn't keep announcing a savings plan after the income that funded it had gone.
fieldNote: Her **income uncertainty** is explicit, so anxiety reflects plausible loss with control rather than an asserted catastrophic outcome requiring a different mood.
The **conditional deposit** stops if essentials are uncovered, and job searches retain written alternatives, adequate paid terms and travel costs.

steps.text: Save 50 extra monthly only while actual earnings cover essentials
Keep actual paid repair work after 2028
Apply for posted maintenance if hours fall, requiring written pay/hours covering bills/travel before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to test a skill against a real job instead of buy every course someone names. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and robots around 2034, so we'd still need to look at both stages. I'd want people to stop pretending one quick class fixes a whole household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own repair wage can hold over the next few years, but the design work at home could change on the way there. We have a three-month buffer and some other electrical employers, which gives us time to compare. I'm still anxious about household income rather than assuming the longer warning makes my partner's customers stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my employer this month about a practical fault-finding workshop linked to our current repair calls. I'd enrol only with a clear place to practise and either employer-covered fees or a 180 fee saved from spare earnings, with no lost paid shifts. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep repair work and review both actual income streams monthly before paying for any further teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but glad not every decision has to happen this week. I like a small course I can connect to work we actually do. I'd still listen if my partner said our own budget made the timing wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if paying the 180 meant drawing on the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait or ask the employer to cover it. The self-funded option is from spare earnings after bills, not a second name for emergency money. If the workshop clashed with a paid shift, I'd choose another date before enrolling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your partner take the same approach to learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd discuss it, but my partner would choose the teaching relevant to the design work. An electrical workshop isn't a plan for my partner's design career. We'd compare any proposal with real costs and time rather than decide enthusiasm was a budget.

say: I'd test **teaching against work** rather than buy every suggested course.
I'd discuss **both stages** and reject claims that one short class fixes an entire household.
think: My **repair wage** looks steady near term, but design orders could change during the preparation years.
Our **buffer and local options** allow comparison without guaranteeing the partner's customers will remain.
do: Ask now about a **fault-finding workshop** linked to current repairs and real practice.
Enrol only with **covered fees** or 180 saved from spare earnings, and no lost paid shifts.
Keep **repair work** after 2031 and review both actual incomes monthly before further course spending.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, with more time to choose an affordable and relevant learning opportunity.
S3.quote: An electrical workshop isn't a plan for my partner's design career.
fieldNote: The **two funding routes** remain explicit: employer payment or 180 from genuine spare earnings, never emergency cash or lost wages.
She does not treat **her training** as protection for the partner's design income, preserving individual choices and household affordability.

steps.text: Take relevant workshop with practice only using covered fees or 180 spare earnings without lost shifts
Keep repairs after 2031 and review actual household incomes before more course spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to make several adjustments and see which ones actually help. I'd still use tools early, but I'd keep checking the money rather than count interest in an idea as income. I'd want the children to have advice and choices, not a family rule about the one safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when thinking AI arrived in 2036 and about 56 when capable robots followed, so retirement isn't something I can assume. My own repair work looks secure for the next few years, but my partner's customer income could still be pressured during that time. The distant endpoint doesn't remove that household worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing actual wages and design receipts monthly now, and seek the workshop only under the same practice, fee and no-lost-wage conditions. I'd add 50 monthly to the reserve only while essentials were covered. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repair work, compare actual job offers before leaving, and stop extra training spending if the household budget fell short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household balance, though less hurried by the machine dates. I'm comfortable changing a plan when the figures change. I'd rather have an honest small plan than an impressive one that assumes my partner never loses a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an actual offer need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Written pay, paid hours, tasks and travel costs that fitted our core bills. I'd ask about new systems and what teaching was provided too. I wouldn't leave paid electrical repairs just because a new job title sounded safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the uncertainty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That learning still matters, and it is sensible to ask what a promise costs. Our children don't have to become electricians or designers to make us proud. I'd rather they practised changing their minds with evidence than chose a course to calm our nerves.

say: I'd use **ten years** for tested adjustments while keeping interest in an idea separate from income.
I'd give the **children** advice and choices rather than name a supposedly safe occupation.
think: I can't assume **retirement** at 53 or when capable robots follow around 56.
My **repair work** looks secure near term, while pressure on design receipts keeps household income on my mind.
do: Review **actual incomes** monthly; take workshops only with practice, employer-covered fees or 180 from spare earnings, and no lost paid shifts.
Save another **50 monthly** only while essentials are covered.
Keep **repairs** after 2036, compare written adequate offers before leaving and stop extra course spending if the budget falls short.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, with less date-driven urgency and willingness to revise plans from real figures.
S4.quote: I wouldn't leave paid electrical repairs just because a new job title sounded safe.
fieldNote: The **long warning** reduces urgency, but her partner's current exposure keeps the mood tied to household rather than solely personal earnings.
The **financial conditions** retain practice, genuine fee funding, protected wages, essential costs and written offers rather than relying on distant optimism.

steps.text: Take relevant workshop only with practice and covered fees or 180 spare earnings without lost shifts
Save 50 extra monthly only after essentials are covered
Keep actual paid repair work after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my partner's design work faces the thinking change first, then robots around 2031 could affect my physical hours. Honest paid terms, teaching linked to real practice and decisions based on actual receipts would help. I don't need somebody to promise a safe occupation; I need choices that fit the household's money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the two adults in the house face the same sort of change. My screwdriver and my partner's design screen don't run on the same clock. I'd want us asked separately before someone announced the family was ready.

headlineQuote: My screwdriver and my partner's design screen don't run on the same clock.
portrait: Bianca is **43**, an experienced licensed electrician with a vocational certificate, average skill, typical pay and some other local employers.
Her **partner designs menus**, with two school-age children, a mortgage and three months saved; design receipts fund extras beyond her core wage.
She uses **AI daily** and tests tools openly, while recognising that household income can shrink through work different from her own.
Her **workshop and saving plans** depend on real practice, affordable fees, protected shifts and essentials being covered rather than assumed future receipts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens the partner's design work before robots around 2031 could also reduce her physical repair hours.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **paid terms** and teaching tied to real practice would create usable choices.
Decisions based on **actual receipts** would keep the household budget distinct from hopes about future work.
